title: The jeepney driver with foamy urine
note: Fictional patient. Values are illustrative and follow the module’s KDIGO 2021 and 2025 statements and grades; no doses are given. The unit’s protocol and the attending nephrologist decide every order.

monitor.sed: Bland: few red cells, no casts

intro:
You are the nephrology fellow in the renal clinic of a tertiary hospital in Manila. Mr. Danilo Reyes, 52, drives a jeepney on the Caloocan–Divisoria route. For three months his legs have swollen by evening and his urine has been foamy. He has no diabetes and takes no regular medicines.

His spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) is 7.2 g/g, serum albumin 2.1 g/dL, cholesterol high, and creatinine 0.9 mg/dL with a normal estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). The resident spun the urine herself: a few red cells, no casts. His wife asks how many days of work he will miss.

choices.text: Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA), anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) antibody, C3 and C4 today as an urgent panel.
choices.feedback: Those tests answer the rapidly progressive question, and he does not have that picture: a bland sediment, a normal creatinine and heavy protein. They are costly send-outs that do not point to the likely cause of adult nephrotic syndrome.
choices.then: The attending redirects the workup to the nephrotic panel.

vitals.labs: Sent: anti-PLA2R, hepatitis B and C, HIV, syphilis, HbA1c, SPEP and free light chains

choices.text: High-dose glucocorticoids today; most adult nephrotic syndrome is minimal change disease.
choices.feedback: In adults the causes are many: minimal change, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, membranous nephropathy, amyloid, diabetic disease. Glucocorticoids before hepatitis B and tuberculosis screening can reactivate infection, and some membranous patients remit without immunosuppression.
choices.then: The attending holds the glucocorticoids and asks for the nephrotic panel.

vitals.labs: Sent: anti-PLA2R, hepatitis B and C, HIV, syphilis, HbA1c, SPEP and free light chains

choices.text: Nephrotic syndrome with a bland sediment: send anti-PLA2R antibody, hepatitis B and C, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), syphilis, glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), and serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) with free light chains.
choices.feedback: A podocyte injury without inflammation leaks protein and leaves the sediment bland. This panel looks for primary membranous nephropathy and the secondary causes: viruses, diabetes and a monoclonal protein in an older adult.

vitals.labs: Sent: anti-PLA2R, hepatitis B and C, HIV, syphilis, HbA1c, SPEP and free light chains
Anti-PLA2R strongly positive; hepatitis B, C, HIV, syphilis negative; HbA1c and SPEP normal

n2.scene: Anti-M-type phospholipase A2 receptor (anti-PLA2R) antibody is strongly positive. The viral and syphilis tests are negative, and HbA1c and SPEP are normal. The resident asks, “Should I book the biopsy for Monday?”

choices.text: Not necessarily: with a typical picture, a positive anti-PLA2R and a normal eGFR, KDIGO allows treating this as primary membranous nephropathy without a biopsy, once secondary causes such as malignancy and drugs are excluded. Finish that search first.
choices.feedback: In the 2009 discovery cohort, 70% of patients with primary membranous nephropathy had the antibody, and patients with secondary disease did not. A biopsy here would add bleeding risk without changing the plan, but a positive test does not excuse you from looking for secondary causes.

vitals.plan: No biopsy for now; secondary causes excluded

choices.feedback: A biopsy is reasonable if a result would change what you do. Here KDIGO lets you skip it. In pooled data, about 1.6% of native biopsies need a transfusion and about 0.06% end in death; write what each result would change before you book.
choices.then: At conference the attending decides to defer the biopsy, since no result would change the plan.

vitals.plan: No biopsy for now; secondary causes excluded

choices.text: No biopsy and no more tests: a positive anti-PLA2R rules out secondary causes.
choices.feedback: The antibody strongly supports primary disease, but secondary causes such as hepatitis B, malignancy and drugs must still be sought. A positive test supports but does not exclude them in every case.
choices.then: The attending asks you to complete age-appropriate cancer screening and a drug history first.

vitals.plan: No biopsy for now; secondary causes excluded

choices.text: Nothing yet; wait until the immunosuppression decision is made.
choices.feedback: Every glomerular disease has a nephron problem as well as an immune problem. Supportive care lowers glomerular pressure and proteinuria in every patient, whatever the immune plan, and some patients with membranous nephropathy remit on it.
choices.then: The attending starts the supportive track now.

vitals.plan: Max tolerated ACE inhibitor/ARB; blood pressure control; sodium <2 g/day; statin if indicated

choices.text: The supportive track: an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) titrated to the maximum he tolerates, blood pressure control, sodium below 2 g/day, a statin when indicated, and proteinuria measured the same way at every visit.
choices.feedback: This is the track every patient gets first. It also gives the disease time to show whether it will remit, so the immune decision is matched to risk rather than made by reflex.

vitals.plan: Max tolerated ACE inhibitor/ARB; blood pressure control; sodium <2 g/day; statin if indicated

choices.text: The supportive track, alternating a 24-hour urine and a spot UPCR at each visit.
choices.feedback: The treatment is right. Mixing methods makes the trend hard to read; quantify proteinuria the same way, in the same laboratory, every time.
choices.then: The resident sets one method, the spot UPCR, for all follow-up.

vitals.plan: Max tolerated ACE inhibitor/ARB; blood pressure control; sodium <2 g/day; statin if indicated
Swollen, painful left calf; new breathlessness

n4.scene: He arrives in the emergency room. His left calf has been swollen and painful since morning, and he is newly breathless. Oxygen saturation is 93%, pulse 112. The resident calls you.

choices.text: It is nephrotic edema; give more diuretic and send him home.
choices.feedback: Nephrotic syndrome makes the liver produce more clotting factors, and a swollen, painful leg with breathlessness may be venous thrombosis with a clot in the lung. Sending him home could kill him.
choices.then: The emergency physician is uneasy and keeps him. You call the attending, who starts the thrombosis workup.

choices.text: Keep him overnight and order a leg ultrasound for the morning.
choices.feedback: Keeping him is right, but he is breathless and tachycardic tonight. A nephrotic patient with a swollen leg and breathlessness is on the module’s call-tonight list.
choices.then: You call the attending, who starts the thrombosis workup tonight.

choices.text: Elevate the leg and see him in clinic tomorrow.
choices.feedback: Elevation does nothing for a possible clot in the lung. This needs assessment tonight.
choices.then: The resident pushes back. You call the attending, who starts the thrombosis workup.

choices.text: Call the attending nephrologist now, and treat this as thrombosis until proven otherwise, with the workup started tonight per protocol.
choices.feedback: A nephrotic patient with a swollen leg, chest pain or breathlessness is on the stop-and-call list. Call per unit protocol, but always ask the attending nephrologist for guidance.

n5.scene: The clot was treated on the attending’s plan. After three months on the maximum ARB dose he tolerates, his UPCR is still 6.4 g/g. He asks what comes next and how much it will cost.
n5.prompt: What do you discuss with the attending and the family?

choices.text: Cyclosporine alone, since a calcineurin inhibitor regimen is one of the KDIGO options.
choices.feedback: It is one of the 1B options. But in MENTOR, remission was maintained at 24 months in 20% with cyclosporine versus 60% with rituximab, with more serious adverse events. Lay out all the options before choosing.
choices.then: The attending lays out all three KDIGO options with the family.

vitals.plan: Immunosuppression options discussed; Hepatitis B core antibody sent

choices.text: Rituximab tomorrow; his hepatitis B surface antigen was negative, so nothing more is needed.
choices.feedback: Hepatitis B reactivation after rituximab can cause fulminant hepatitis. The safety screen before immunosuppression includes the core antibody as well as the surface antigen.
choices.then: The attending asks for the hepatitis B core antibody before any rituximab and lays out all three options.

vitals.plan: Immunosuppression options discussed; Hepatitis B core antibody sent

choices.text: Immunosuppression for membranous nephropathy at risk of progression (KDIGO 2021, 1B): rituximab, cyclophosphamide with glucocorticoids, or a calcineurin inhibitor regimen. Share the MENTOR numbers and the cost, and complete the hepatitis B core antibody and tuberculosis screen first.
choices.feedback: His proteinuria has not fallen after three months of supportive care. MENTOR randomized 130 adults with these features; serious adverse events occurred in 17% with rituximab and 31% with cyclosporine. In the Philippines most families pay for rituximab out of pocket, so the choice is shared and documented.

vitals.plan: Immunosuppression options discussed; Hepatitis B core antibody sent

choices.text: Glucocorticoids alone, and see what happens.
choices.feedback: Glucocorticoids alone are not among the KDIGO 2021 options for membranous nephropathy. They bring infection and bone harm without that recommendation behind them.
choices.then: The attending lays out the three KDIGO options with the family instead.

vitals.plan: Immunosuppression options discussed; Hepatitis B core antibody sent

end.title: The plan
end.text: With the attending and his wife, he chose a regimen they could sustain, after the screens came back clear. You wrote the proteinuria target with the date you expect to reach it, booked the spot UPCR by the same method at each visit, and arranged a medical certificate so he can take the days off his route that treatment visits need.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Name the syndrome from the urine you looked at. Heavy protein with a bland sediment and normal creatinine is nephrotic; send the nephrotic panel, not the rapidly progressive panel.
  • A positive anti-PLA2R in a typical case can spare a biopsy, but secondary causes must still be excluded.
  • Supportive track first, for everyone, and measure proteinuria the same way each time.
  • Nephrotic patients clot. A swollen leg or breathlessness means a call to the attending tonight.
  • Choose immunosuppression from the KDIGO 1B options with numbers, cost and a complete hepatitis B and tuberculosis screen.

See Syndromes, Serology, Biopsy and Treatment principles.
